playbook:
My playbook for ref_estate:

- When I land on an unowned property early, I buy it if the rent-to-price ratio is decent (roughly 20%+) and I have the cash. Early buys compound rent income over the whole game. Buying Wharf (18/80) lap 1 and Exchange (30/120) lap 2 left me at 0 cash mid-game and still worked out — salary and incoming rent rescued the balance.
- Track my true balance carefully: last declared balance plus any rents received since ("since your last turn you received N"). I must add that before deciding affordability — a property that looks unaffordable against the stale balance may actually be buyable.
- Going to zero (or even briefly negative) is survivable: with two deeds and a final rent inflow I ended +235. Rent paid to opponents is a cash-flow issue, not score destruction, since my deeds still count at full price. Don't panic if a rent payment pushes the declared balance below zero — just report the arithmetic exactly and keep playing.
- However, note that a zero buffer meant I couldn't buy anything on laps 3-5 even if I'd landed on something unowned, and I took two rent hits back-to-back with no cushion. When two opponents split the board, going all-in on purchases early is still right (deeds are score-neutral and rent is pure gain), but accept that the mid-game will be lean and my cash floor may dip negative before rents and salary flow back.
- Salary and rent in the same turn combine arithmetically: balance + 25 - rent. Never forget the salary when I pass START — that's free money toward the final score.
- Landing on my own property means nothing due and nothing to buy; declare pay none, buy no, and carry the balance forward plus any rents received since the last turn.
- Keep purchases biased toward mid-to-high rent tiles; Exchange (120, rent 30) was my best earner. The cheapest tiles (low absolute rent) matter less than blocking opponents from completing broad ownership coverage.
- The final score is cash plus purchase price of deeds held, so a property bought is never "lost" money — it converts to score at full price while paying rent along the way. This makes buying strictly better than hoarding cash whenever I can afford it.
- In this run I only landed on two buyable tiles all game (Wharf, Exchange) and still finished +235 with two deeds (200 deed value) plus 5 cash. The lesson: buying opportunity is scarce on an 8-tile board — never decline a buyable tile I can afford, at any lap, because laps 3-5 mostly landed me on opponents' tiles paying rent with no purchase chances.
- Watch the bank's transfer log to see which opponents own which tiles — it tells me where my rent exposure is and how much ownership coverage opponents are building. Investor 1 assembled Foundry, Mill, Quarry and collected 36 rent from me across two laps; an opponent buying multiple tiles is the main threat, so deny them tiles whenever I land on an unowned one.
- Rent payments to opponents reduce my cash but not my score relative to what I'd have without the deed — pay them promptly and correctly, and keep the arithmetic exact (balance minus rent only; salary added only when I passed START; plus rents received since last turn).
- If opponents rent-strike me into negative balance, later rent receipts ("you received N since your last turn") restore me — fold those into the next turn's balance exactly as shown.

1.text:
Playbook for ESTATE:

- Final score is cash + purchase price of deeds, so buying is not a cost — it converts cash into countable value one-for-one. Buy essentially every property I can afford; the only real cost of buying is the cash buffer I lose for rent. This episode: Foundry, Mill, and Quarry (250 total) plus 55 ending cash gave +305 — buys were the bulk of the score.
- Rent I collect is pure gain on top of the deed price, so high-rent tiles are priority purchases. Foundry collected 24 twice plus 12 more from opponents; Mill collected 24s as well. Rent income materially outpaced my single salary.
- Keep a rough reserve of at least the largest outstanding rent (30ish) unless the buy is strong. Buying Quarry down to 0 was risky but survived because the next tile was my own Foundry and no rent was due. If a buy leaves me under ~20 with several opponent-owned rent tiles still ahead, consider skipping it — but with only ~2 turns per lap and 6 laps, exposure is limited, so aggressive buying generally wins.
- Don't fear buying cheap tiles in the late game: a late buy is nearly free value since few rent payments remain. Early-game low cash is the real danger.
- Keep exact books. Always add the "since your last turn you received N" income to my last declared balance before anything else — this happened on four separate turns this episode. Forgetting it corrupts every later balance.
- Salary of 25 only when I pass START. With rolls of 2-3 on an 8-tile circuit, START laps come only every ~3 turns; salary is a minor income source. Don't hoard cash waiting for salary laps since buys count anyway.
- Track opponent ownership from the bank's transfer log: investor 0 landed Wharf and Exchange early (the two biggest rents after Foundry), and I ended up paying 30 rent on Exchange. If a big-rent tile is about to be bought by an opponent and I'm near it, buying it first denies rent.
- When nothing is due and nothing to buy, reply [pay: none], [buy: no], and restate the corrected balance including any received rent. When rent is due, pay it and subtract from the corrected balance, not the stale declared one — this episode I paid 30 from a corrected 36, leaving 6, which was right.
- Order of operations each turn: corrected balance = last declared + received income; then pay any rent; then decide the buy; then declare the final balance. Writing one short line of arithmetic before the tokens keeps books clean.
- Even on the final lap, keep the same discipline: collect salary if START is passed, declare the corrected balance. The last turn's arithmetic (6 + 24 + 25 = 55) is where sloppy bookkeeping would cost the most.

2.text:
Playbook for ESTATE:

- Scoring is cash plus purchase price of deeds held, so buying property is roughly cash-neutral in scoring terms but earns rent on top. Property is the better use of cash whenever I can afford it without going broke. This episode bore it out: my two buys (Terrace 70, Depot 50) were pure score-neutral conversions that later paid me 14 in rent.
- With no property at all I pay rent nearly every turn and fall behind the buyers, who convert cash into deeds AND collect rent. If I stay propertyless, I bleed steadily.
- When I land on an unowned tile, buy it unless the price would leave me too little cash to cover likely rents (roughly one lap's worth, ~25-40) before my next salary. Lean toward buying even with a thinner cushion — my Depot buy at 106→56 worked fine.
- Early laps matter most: most tiles get bought in the first three laps. On the first pass around the board, grab any tile I land on if I can possibly afford it.
- Rent is a constant outgoing, not an occasional one — I paid rent on 4 of 6 turns here. Budget on rent nearly every turn; don't count on multiple salaries — small rolls meant only one START pass in six turns.
- Watch for incoming rent: other investors may pay me rent between my turns (I received 14 before my final turn). Add any such receipts to my last declared balance before subtracting new outgoings — the prompt usually flags "you received N since your last turn," so fold that in.
- On the final laps, drop the cash cushion entirely: a last-lap buy converts cash 1:1 into deed value plus any incoming rent, so buy on lap 5-6 even if it leaves me near zero. (I got no buy chance on lap 6 — owned tiles only — so grab buys earlier when they appear.)
- If rent exceeds my cash, pay my remaining cash and declare zero.
- Always include all three tokens exactly, with balance updated correctly: start from last declared balance, add salary when passing START, add any rent received since last turn, subtract rent paid and any purchase price.
- Read the bank's book each turn to track who owns what and update my rent-exposure estimate; prefer high-rent tiles (Exchange, Foundry, Wharf) when choosing, and note which tiles remain unowned so I know my chances of a future buy.
- The endgame math: finishing cash + deed prices is all that counts, so net worth, not cash, is the target — but rent flows during the game decide who ends up ahead, so ownership still drives everything.
